turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Jordan. I'm Priya, I'll do your obs before Dr Nguyen comes in. Sleeve up for me, thanks.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, no worries. Sorry I'm a bit all over the place, I nearly didn't come because I reckoned it was nothing, but my partner Sam basically frogmarched me, said the heart thing's been freaking them out, and I was like it's fine, it's just when I've had too many coffees, but then last night it went on for ages and I couldn't get back to sleep and—
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): We'll get the numbers first, then you can tell the doctor the whole story. Blood pressure's one twenty-eight over seventy-eight.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that bad? My watch sometimes yells at me. It said one-forty the other night, but I think the watch is dodgy when I'm moving around in bed, so I don't really trust it.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Watch readings can jump about. Pulse is a hundred and twelve... sorry, I misread the screen, it's ninety-four. Sitting still, that's the one I'll write down.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ninety-four doesn't sound that high. When it happens it's way faster, like I can't count it, and my chest feels hollow, not painful exactly, more like—
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Temp's thirty-six point six, oxygen ninety-eight percent, and you're breathing at sixteen. That's all fine just now. The doctor—

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, sixteen what, breaths? Because when it hits I feel like I'm not getting a proper breath in, especially at night, and also before exams, I've got two coming up, and before the Monday meetings at work, I do admin at a physio clinic three days and uni the other days, occupational therapy, second year, so it's heaps, but I don't think it's stress, I handle stress fine.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Breaths per minute, yep. While you were checking in, Sam mentioned to me at the desk that you've been close to passing out a couple of times. I should pass that on.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's not right. I've never felt like I was going to faint. Sam worries, I just get puffed and my heart goes, I haven't blacked out, not even close.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hi Jordan, I'm Dr Nguyen. I've had a quick look at those obs Priya just did. What brought you in today?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): So the main thing is my heart racing, palpitations I guess you'd call them, and I get short of breath with it. It's been going on since last winter, or maybe the winter before that, around the footy finals or after, I honestly couldn't tell you a month.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Last winter or the one before. We'll leave the start date loose for now. How often is the racing happening at the moment?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I was going to say a couple of times a week, but that's not honest. It's more like four or five nights a week, and then again if I've got an exam or a work meeting that day. Nights are the worst.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): Four or five nights a week, worse at night, and also before exams or meetings. And the breathlessness, does it—
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry, the coffee, I have to say the coffee before I lose the number.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, hang on, you asked about the breathing. It comes with the racing, not really on its own, and it eases if I sit up and wait it out. Sometimes twenty minutes, sometimes longer.
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): So they come together, and sitting up helps. We'll do the coffee in a minute. Any chest pain with it?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No pain. It's a flutter and a hollow feeling, not a pain, and it doesn't go down my arm or anything.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): Good. And have you actually lost consciousness, even for a second?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, never. Like I said to Priya, Sam's got that wrong. I stay awake the whole time.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Okay. You and Sam don't agree on the near-fainting. Any fever, or a cough, or swelling in the ankles?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, no cough. Ankles are normal. I look, because my nanna had swollen ankles with her heart, but mine are fine.
[SEG0024] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in, the ECG machine's free after you've finished chatting. I'll be out the front.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thanks Priya, I'll send Jordan out once we're done talking.
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to take my jumper off for that? I wore layers and it's a pain, not that it matters, I just—
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): They'll sort the top half. Anything that sets the episodes off, besides the night-time and the meetings?

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Coffee, and those energy drinks from the servo. I told myself it was four coffees a day, but if I'm honest it's six, easy, long blacks mostly, and then two energy drinks, sometimes three if uni goes late.
[SEG0029] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six coffees and two to three energy drinks. That's a fair caffeine load. Do you vape, or smoke?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. I don't smoke cigarettes, never really did, maybe a few at parties years ago. The vape I've had for two years... actually closer to three years, a nicotine one, mango, which is ridiculous at twenty-four.
[SEG0031] person_3 (DOCTOR): Vaping about three years, nicotine, not cigarettes now. You also said you don't think stress is part of this.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah nah, I don't feel stressed. I just get organised, I'm not anxious, I sleep alright apart from when the palpitations wake me. Sam says I look wound up, I don't feel wound up.
[SEG0033] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll record that you don't experience it as anxiety, even though the timing sits around exams and meetings. What are you taking, any tablets?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Magnesium, from the chemist. I thought it was two hundred milligrams, but the jar this morning says four hundred milligrams, one at night, for the flutters. I forget it half the time, so I couldn't swear I'm taking it properly.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Four hundred milligrams at night, when you remember. Anything a doctor prescribed?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): The GP in Brunswick gave me propranolol. I thought the dose was twenty-five milligrams, no, and I nearly said forty, but forty was my flatmate's blood pressure tablet, not mine. Mine was ten milligrams, twice a day, and I stopped it.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ten milligrams twice a day, stopped. When did you stop, and why?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Maybe six weeks ago, or longer, I can't pin it. It made me feel flat and a bit dizzy, and I only ever took it when my heart was already going, not twice a day like she said. I haven't had any since.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not taken as prescribed, then stopped, roughly six weeks or more. Any other pills, even one you tried once?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): There's a white tablet Sam bought online for calm. I can't remember the name, something herbal-sounding. I took one, it made me drowsy all afternoon, and I didn't take it again.
[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): An unnamed white tablet, once, then stopped. Any allergies to medicines?

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. Well, actually, I'm not sure. When I was little they thought penicillin, I got a rash, but Mum reckoned it was just the fever, and I've stayed away from it anyway.
[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): A possible penicillin rash, never clarified. Any operations?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none, not even tonsils. I broke my wrist at twelve, footy, but that was a cast, not an operation.
[SEG0045] person_3 (DOCTOR): No surgery. Any ongoing conditions, asthma, thyroid disease, a heart diagnosis of your own?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No asthma, no thyroid that I know of, no heart diagnosis. I get mild eczema on my hands in the winter and it's still a thing, though it's quiet right now.
[SEG0047] person_3 (DOCTOR): Eczema, ongoing, quiet at present. Family history of rhythm problems, or thyroid disease?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Dad's got atrial fibrillation, he's fifty-eight, on a blood thinner I forget the name of. No thyroid in the family that anyone's mentioned.
[SEG0049] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dad with atrial fibrillation. Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): A bit on weekends. Maybe four beers over a Saturday, not through the week. I did dry July once and the heart thing didn't change, so I don't reckon it's the beer.
[SEG0051] person_3 (DOCTOR): About four beers on a Saturday. Who's at home?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I live with Sam in Coburg, three years together. Sam's on a shift today, they made me promise not to downplay this, which I've probably stuffed up already.
[SEG0053] person_3 (DOCTOR): Living with your partner. What about exercise?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I ride to uni most days, about twenty minutes, and the gym's fallen off this semester. The breathlessness isn't on the bike, weirdly, it's when I'm resting.
[SEG0055] person_3 (DOCTOR): Useful, that it's at rest. I'll listen to your chest.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. I'll try to stop talking, which is not my strong suit.

[SEG0057] person_3 (DOCTOR): Heart sounds are normal, regular, no murmur while you're sitting. Lungs are clear, no wheeze. No swelling at the ankles, and your pulse is steady, same as Priya's reading.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): So it looks normal in the chair. I said four or five nights, it just isn't happening this minute.
[SEG0059] person_3 (DOCTOR): The exam is reassuring, but it won't catch the night episodes. Let me say it back.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, go on.

[SEG0061] person_3 (DOCTOR): You're twenty-four, with palpitations and shortness of breath four or five nights a week and before exams or meetings, since last winter or possibly the one before. No chest pain and no true faint that you'll own, though Sam told Priya you'd nearly passed out and you dispute that. Six coffees, energy drinks, vaping about three years, magnesium four hundred when you remember, propranolol ten milligrams stopped. Penicillin is unclear, you've got eczema, and your dad has atrial fibrillation.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): That's fair. Don't write that I'm anxious, I'm not. And the near-fainting is definitely not a thing.

[SEG0063] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't call it an anxiety disorder. My working impression is that the palpitations and breathlessness may well be driven by the caffeine and the vaping, and the timing around exams and meetings still matters, but I need a tracing before I can say what the rhythm is doing, and I want to exclude a thyroid problem. An arrhythmia is less likely given today, but it's not off the table.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): So you don't know yet. I'd rather you didn't guess. What do we actually do?
[SEG0065] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll order an ECG today, Priya can do it on the way out, and thyroid bloods, TSH and free T4.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods today as well? I hate needles, but alright. Do I need to fast, because I had brekkie, a toastie and a coffee, which is a bit on the nose.

[SEG0067] person_3 (DOCTOR): No need to fast for these. When an episode starts, try a breathing exercise, in for four, hold for four, out for six, sitting up. It won't fix a rhythm problem, but it can settle the edge while it passes.
[SEG0068] person_2 (PATIENT): In for four, hold for four, out for six. Sam will turn it into a coaching session, they'll be unbearable, but I'll do it.

[SEG0069] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'd also like the energy drinks gone this fortnight, coffee capped at two a day, and the vape eased off if you can. Then we can see what your heart does without that load.
[SEG0070] person_2 (PATIENT): Two coffees is going to hurt, I'll try. I'm not promising on the vape, that's the hard one, but I can bin the energy drinks, they're expensive anyway.

[SEG0071] person_3 (DOCTOR): Trying is enough. Come back and see me in a fortnight with the results, whether you feel better or not. If you get chest pain, or you actually pass out, go to emergency rather than waiting.
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight. What if the bloods take longer? Last time I had iron studies the lab was slow, not that iron matters here.
[SEG0073] person_3 (DOCTOR): If the results aren't in, reception can move the appointment, but the plan is still two weeks. I don't need a sharper start date if you haven't got one.
[SEG0074] person_2 (PATIENT): I really can't give you one. Last winter, or the winter before, is as close as it gets. Sorry for talking your ear off.
[SEG0075] person_3 (DOCTOR): You gave me what I needed. Priya will do the ECG and the bloods out the front.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): Thanks. I'll try not to have another long black in the waiting room, no promises though.

spec.situation: Young adult with palpitations and breathlessness, worse at night and before exams or work meetings; downplays stress, drinks a lot of coffee and energy drinks, vapes; friend or partner contributes. Doctor orders ECG and thyroid tests, discusses breathing exercises.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Nurse relays Sam's claim, but patient repeatedly denies any near-fainting.
bad.text: Near-fainting (category=neurological, status=present, frequency=a couple of times, temporality=current, reported_by=nurse, certainty=disputed)

omissions.text: Palpitations are described as a fluttering/hollow feeling rather than pain, and there is no radiation down the arm.

The patient denies blackout and specifically says they have never felt like they were going to faint, 'not even close'; the recorded near-fainting symptom as present is misleading despite being marked disputed.
Shortness of breath is described as feeling unable to get a proper breath in, especially at night.
Sleep is otherwise alright apart from being woken by palpitations.

Possible penicillin allergy details are incomplete: the rash occurred in childhood and the patient's mother thought it may have been due to the fever rather than penicillin; the patient has avoided penicillin since.
Past history includes a wrist fracture at age 12 managed with a cast and no operation.
The patient reports no cigarette smoking now and only a few cigarettes at parties years ago.
The patient does not experience breathlessness on the bike/exertion; it occurs at rest.
Cardiac examination was normal and regular specifically while sitting.
Doctor's assessment included that arrhythmia is less likely given today's findings, but not excluded.
Thyroid blood tests do not require fasting.
If test results are not back, reception can move the follow-up appointment; plan remains two weeks.
The doctor stated Priya would do both the ECG and the bloods out the front today.
